title: How to Decide What Work AI Should Do for You: The AI Deputization Audit
dek: Two new features — GrokBot's teach-a-task and ChatGPT's Computer History — mark the moment the AI bottleneck officially moved from capability to context. But once your AI can learn how you work, you still have to decide what work it should actually do. NLW proposes a scoring system: the AI deputization audit.

oneIdea.headline: AI's bottleneck has moved from capability to context — now the question is what you deputize.
oneIdea.summary: GrokBot lets you teach a task by recording yourself doing it; ChatGPT's Computer History watches how you work and learns over time. Deliberate demonstration and ambient observation both solve the same problem: models are capable enough, they just don't know your work. What's left is a decision framework — score each recurring process on frequency, teachability, checkability, stakes, and how much it really needs to be you. Deputize the 8-10s, defend the 0-3s, and duet on everything in the middle, which is where most knowledge work still lives.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: The deputization audit fits a surgery well — until you reach the checkability column
items.body: Inventory the recurring work of a practice and the list writes itself: coding and filing incoming letters, results acknowledgement, medication query triage, recall and QOF chasing, drafting routine referrals, insurance and DWP report first drafts, the endless summarising. Score those on NLW's five dimensions and most sit in his middle tier, because the third criterion — how long checking takes against doing — behaves differently in clinical work. A referral letter that reads well but has the wrong laterality costs more to miss than it saved to draft, and the responsible clinician signs it either way, so the check cannot be delegated with the task. That is the honest reason a scribe has been transformative while more ambitious hand-offs have not: the scribe produces something I was going to read carefully in any case.

items.title: Ambient observation is the wrong shape for a consulting-room desktop
items.body: A tool that watches everything you do across every application, and learns from it, is a very different information governance proposition in a surgery than in a marketing department. The screen holds other patients' records, open pathology, safeguarding notes and correspondence about third parties, and a continuous capture of interaction events is still processing of special category data that needs a DPIA, a clear lawful basis, and DCB0129/0160 clinical safety assurance from the supplier. Deliberate demonstration — you decide to record one workflow, on synthetic or your own test data — is much easier to justify than passive observation, and it is the option I would ask about first. If NLW is right that ambient context is where the real gains are, then practices will need suppliers to answer the governance questions properly rather than shipping a consumer feature into the NHS by the back door.

items.title: Cost the experiment at the price it will be, not the price it is
items.body: NLW closes by suggesting the price of these agent tools will come down as access widens. Zitron's counter is that buyers have never seen the true cost, and that the arrival of real billing produced spending caps rather than enthusiasm. For a practice deciding whether to build a workflow around any of this, the two positions converge on the same prudent question to a supplier: what does this cost per unit of work, and what happens to that figure when the current pricing ends? A scribe subscription that is affordable at one price and unaffordable at three times it is a workflow risk as much as a budget one, and the mitigation is the dull one — do not build a process you could not run without the tool for a fortnight.

the_other_side.text: NLW's lead is that models are now capable enough, the missing ingredient is context, and the sensible response is an audit that hands recurring work over. Zitron's nearest published argument attacks the arithmetic underneath that audit: he says nobody can measure the return on AI, or even "create a standard measurement of the cost of a task", because outputs are hallucination-prone and every harness behaves differently. His evidence is billing rather than benchmarks — GitHub Copilot users burning a third of a month's credits in a few hours once token pricing arrived, Uber's COO saying the spend was getting harder to justify, Walmart and Amazon telling staff to stop using AI for its own sake. And on the point NLW calls checkability, Zitron's position is that the vigilance never ends: a model with no ability to learn outside training can go wrong unpredictably on any given run, so the human stays in the loop indefinitely.

the_truth_beneath.text: Both men orbit one variable: the cost of checking work you have handed over, and whether that cost falls as the machine learns how you work. They agree on more than the framing admits — that most delegable work is dull and recurring, that output must be verified, and that users have been shielded from what a task really costs. The empirical question is whether verification and cost per task fall as observed context accumulates; the observable that settles it is organisations publishing before-and-after error rates and per-task spend on a specific deputized process, rather than adoption anecdotes. The residue is worldview: Whittemore reads a solvable context gap, Zitron an unmeasurable product sold on obscured pricing. Whittemore is vindicated if recurring processes run on spot checks at stable cost; Zitron if checking still takes as long as doing and bills keep surprising people. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is their shared premise that checkability decides everything. Watch for the first honest published per-task cost and error rate on a deputized workflow.

headlines.headline: Google ships Gemini 3.7 Flash — and it's built for speed
headlines.summary: Not the delayed 3.5 Pro or the anticipated Gemini 4, but a play in a different category: efficiency. At 340 tokens per second it's more than twice as fast as GPT-56 and even edges NVIDIA's new Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, with solid gains on the DeepSwee coding benchmark and prices cut in half.

headlines.headline: Flash sits in an uncomfortable middle ground on cost-per-intelligence
headlines.summary: Even after the price cut, 3.7 Flash costs 40 cents per task on the Artificial Analysis run — the same as MuSpark, more than Nemotron 3 Ultra or GLM 5.2, and around eight times more than ultra-cheap models like GPT 56-Luna. Most users are either paying a little more for a frontier model or looking for something much cheaper.

headlines.headline: The counter-case: for interactive coding, Flash's speed changes the math
headlines.summary: Vercel's Brandon Galang says to ignore the FUD — 3.7 Flash sits on the Pareto frontier once you account for 5.6 Luna being a much smaller model — and analyst Max Weinbach is enjoying it in Anti-Gravity with 'insanely high' usage limits. For partially synchronous coding, where you sit and interact with the agent's output, speed can justify a premium even below frontier performance.

headlines.headline: The 'model race' is branching into multiple races
headlines.summary: There's still a race for the frontier — but also races for distribution, harnesses, and revenue. Within models alone, Google is betting speed is a dimension people will pay attention to, and the massive efficiency boost also makes 3.7 Flash a big upgrade for Gemini Spark, Google's personal agent.

headlines.headline: Switching to a cheaper Chinese model won't necessarily save you money
headlines.summary: An Alpha Sense study ran US and Chinese models through hundreds of real-world financial-analysis tasks. GPT 5.6 Sol completed the work around 13% cheaper than Kimi K3 with roughly 20% higher quality, while US open-weight models Gemma 4 and Inkling matched GLM 5.2's quality at less than one-fifth the cost. Sonnet 5 was the outlier: lower quality than Opus 4.8 at more than five times the price.

headlines.headline: Some of the more expensive models actually ended up being less costly because they were more efficient in using tokens.
headlines.summary: The message for enterprise buyers and planners: price per token is a deceptive metric. The faster conventional wisdom shifts toward measuring efficiency on your actual tasks, the better off your budget will be.

headlines.headline: OpenAI answers on speed: ultra fast mode for GPT-56 Sol
headlines.summary: The company claims frontier intelligence at fourteen times the speed — 750 tokens per second, more than double Gemini 3.7 Flash — leveraging its Cerebras optimizations. API-only for select customers, pitched at latency-sensitive work like real-time voice, commerce, coding, financial research, and security response. No word on the premium, but presumably it's not ultra cheap.

headlines.headline: OpenAI's CRO exits after nine months — the third senior departure in months
headlines.summary: Denise Dresser, the Salesforce veteran and former Slack CEO brought in to ease investor concerns, is leaving; former Wiz president and COO Dolly Rajak replaces her. Coming days after Brad Lightcap's exit and following Fiji Simo's July departure, it looks like a pattern — and Axios sources suggest President Greg Brockman has been building up his own team of leaders.

headlines.headline: Nine times out of ten, the Occam's razor explanation for personnel moves is personal
headlines.summary: There's an outsized appetite right now to read every executive shift as a tea leaf for major problems inside OpenAI, and analyzing from outside is fraught. Still, the market is noticing — turnover is being flagged as a pre-IPO problem, though with the listing now delayed to next year, there's plenty of time to build another narrative.

headlines.headline: The bottleneck in AI has moved from capability to context
headlines.summary: Two features launched this week make the shift concrete: just because a model can do something doesn't mean it has the information it needs to do it well relative to you personally. The new tools attack that gap directly — by watching you work.

headlines.headline: GrokBot lets you teach it a task by recording yourself doing it
headlines.summary: In Cursor and SpaceX AI's simplified take on Open Claw, you hit a plus button in chat, record yourself doing something in the browser, and the bot watches — then theoretically can do it again. The Cursor team says many things GrokBot handles on its own, but if it's struggling, teaching it a task solves the problem in one fell swoop.

headlines.headline: ChatGPT's Computer History learns from everything you do on a computer
headlines.summary: Per OpenAI's Ari Weinstein, it lets ChatGPT understand how you work, finish tasks you're in the middle of, and suggest skills and automations based on how you use your machine. Same goal as GrokBot's teach-a-task: show the AI how you work so it can do more of it.

headlines.headline: This is Windows Recall — except this time people want it
headlines.summary: Microsoft's 2024 screenshot-everything feature was branded a privacy nightmare and had to be recalled and reworked. Now users are openly handing AI their history, medical records, and bank statements, and creators who quietly wanted Recall are saying so out loud. Part of it is shifting privacy attitudes; a technical difference helps too — as Simon Smith notes, Computer History records interaction events, not screens or audio.

headlines.headline: What changed isn't just privacy norms — it's the value proposition
headlines.summary: Microsoft pitched Recall as solving 'finding something you've seen before on your PC' — not a big enough problem to risk the privacy trade. An AI agent that actually does your work for you is a much different value proposition, and now there's real choice in how agents get the context they need.

headlines.headline: Two paradigms for AI learning your work: ambient observation vs. deliberate demonstration
headlines.summary: Computer History is ambient — it watches across apps and builds context without effort on your part, which for many will be the killer feature. GrokBot's teach-a-task is deliberate — you intentionally decide 'I am going to teach you this skill,' show the workflow, and it saves the steps as a repeatable routine. Both patterns have real constituencies.

headlines.headline: Deputize, don't automate
headlines.summary: The word choice is intentional: deputizing AI to go do something in your stead is a different relationship than automating a task away and never thinking about it again. That framing shapes the whole audit.

headlines.headline: Step one: inventory your recurring processes
headlines.summary: No matter how novel we want our work to be, a lot of it is stuff done day in, day out: email triage, weekly status reports, meeting prep, research briefs, CRM hygiene, content repurposing, scheduling, vendor portal chores, inbound lead qualification, metrics pulls. Recurring work is what deputization is built for.

headlines.headline: Score each process 0-2 on five dimensions
headlines.summary: One: is it worth it — how often does it happen and how long does it take? Two: teachability — could you show it in a ten-minute screen share? Three: checkability — how long does verifying the output take versus doing it? Four: stakes — how bad is it if the AI gets it wrong and nobody catches it? Five: how much you personally are the key factor in the output's quality.

headlines.headline: Three tiers: deputize (8-10), duet (4-7), defend (0-3)
headlines.summary: Eight-plus means low stakes, high frequency, highly teachable, and it doesn't need to be you — hand it over, spot check, and start there with Computer History or GrokBot. Zero to three means keep it: mistakes are expensive or the person on the other end expects you. The catch is that most knowledge work today falls in the duet middle — and the real question is whether AI learns well enough over time to move duets into deputized.

headlines.headline: For everything you can't hand off, name the specific blocker
headlines.summary: Because new tools change the equation blocker by blocker. Work trapped in legacy software with no API? Computer-use agents that click the same screens you do dissolve that. Processes you know how to do but can't write down? Now you can show rather than tell. Missing context might be solved by Computer History's ongoing observation — but probably not by a ten-minute GrokBot demo.

headlines.headline: Some blockers survive — and the new tools even create one
headlines.summary: Work requiring taste or judgment, costly or irreversible mistakes, and tasks that depend on human relationships aren't solved by teach-a-task capabilities. And if privacy or security was the blocker, these tools can add one: recording your screen creates a new thing to secure.

headlines.headline: GrokBot's day-two reviews: great for beginners, limiting for power users
headlines.summary: Superintelligent trainer Nufar Gaspar found GrokBot is good for people who haven't built complete agent systems yet, but advanced users hit walls — no control over which folder holds the relevant context, no model choice. If you've been through Claw Camp, it may not be a perfect fit.

headlines.headline: Early GrokBot patterns: topic-per-bot with a chief of staff on top
headlines.summary: John O'Neill, who owns a plumbing company, went from zero to automated dispatch and office chores in 24 hours with no engineers on payroll. Many users spin up individual bots for individual tasks but interact only through a main chief-of-staff bot that coordinates the rest — an early emerging best practice.

headlines.headline: The universal starter job: inbox/Slack tracker and morning brief
headlines.summary: Matt Van Horne notes it's the same first job as for every agent generation before — except now it takes about a minute to set up. A good low-risk first experiment for anyone with GrokBot or Computer History access.

headlines.headline: The biggest barrier is carving out time to work differently
headlines.summary: Even highly AI-forward people struggle here — especially high-productivity workers whose workflows are so dialed in that changing them feels like a short-term waste of time, even when it would save a lot of time in the long run. The experiments are worth it; watch for GrokBot's cost to come down as access expands.
